Want to graduate? Want to become a Doctor? Then read on! With just a thesis of a hundred-plus pages, graduation need not be a dream! ~~End of momentary madness.~~

:::

## ITS: Intention to Submit {#its-intention-to-submit}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

Q: Is ITS important? I am busy writing my thesis. Can I leave it for now?

A: If the timing of graduation matters to you, be sure to submit the ITS form early! ITS starts the entire thesis and viva process. Under the current rules, you may submit your thesis only **at least two months after submitting ITS**. Later is allowed; earlier is not. After submitting ITS, you must submit the thesis within one year. This operates alongside your own thesis deadline, with the earlier deadline applying.

Q: What goes into ITS?

A: Your thesis title, abstract, and basic personal information. The title and abstract do not need to be final; they can be changed later.

Q: Can I just make up a title and abstract to get the form out of the way?

A: Your supervisor and the Graduate School use the title and abstract to choose your internal and external examiners, who will also receive them. They can differ from the final version, but should still reflect your research over the past few years as accurately as possible.

Q: I have more questions.

A: First read the official documents: <https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/aqsd/academic-codes-of-practice/pgr-code-of-practice/>.

:::

## The thesis {#thesis-学位论文毕业论文}

### Format and typesetting {#格式和排版}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

Official document: <https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/media/livacuk/tqsd/code-of-practice-on-assessment/annex-7.1-PGR-CoP.pdf>. Use this as the authority whenever you are unsure about formatting. Below are questions that recur constantly in the WeChat group.

Q: What software can I use to write the thesis?

A: According to the rules above, Liverpool does not prescribe software, so you can use whatever you prefer. Common choices are Microsoft Word and LaTeX.

Q: What do you recommend?

A: LaTeX has several advantages: (1) entering equations is very convenient; (2) references and citations are easy to manage without external software such as EndNote; (3) the formatting is attractive and consistent, making ugly typesetting difficult; and (4) files are small and can be split up for convenient backups. Its disadvantage is the relatively steep learning curve. If your field uses Word rather than LaTeX for journal and conference papers, switching will take some time to learn.

Q: The formatting document has so many detailed requirements. Please, please give me a thesis template!

A:

1. There really is an official Word template, available from this project's fileshare: <https://gitee.com/kaiwu-astro/xp_pgrs_unofficial_guide/tree/main/fileshare>. Source: a teacher on the ELC Thesis Writing Camp.

2. There is no official LaTeX template, but most School of Mathematics and Physics (SMP) graduates have written their theses in LaTeX. Search Overleaf's template gallery for "Liverpool Thesis". There should be just one result, which you can use.

3. Template users, pay special attention: never fully trust the template! The Word template came from an XJTLU ELC teacher, not Liverpool, and the Overleaf template is unofficial. In principle, neither is **responsible** for your thesis or graduation. On obtaining a template, the first step is always to open the Code of Practice above and check every requirement against it.

:::

### Word count {#字数}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

Q: The Code of Practice only states a maximum word count. What is the minimum?

A: Another constantly recurring question. I once asked a teacher at the Graduate School's Thesis Writing Camp. His view was that, since XJTLU master's theses have a maximum of 30,000 words, a PhD thesis should preferably exceed that. But I later found this was not really the case. I have seen theses shorter than 100 pages and others close to 200 pages, all of whose authors graduated. Across the university, there truly is no fixed requirement. If you still want a rough minimum for peace of mind, download theses from the Liverpool and XJTLU libraries. Focus on your school, department, and subject, ideally theses by graduates from your own research group, and see their word and page counts. **Remember: more words do not guarantee an easy graduation.** A senior student's thesis was close to 200 pages and received major corrections; the external examiner said it was too long and read like a textbook.

(Information dated: 12 August 2024)

:::

## The viva {#论文答辩}

### The process before and after the viva {#答辩前后流程}

::: {.contribution authors="ziwen-xie"}

1. At least two months before formally submitting the thesis on e-Bridge, your supervisor selects proposed examiners and submits the list to XJTLU pgsupport and Liverpool for approval.

2. After the thesis is formally submitted on e-Bridge, the university contacts the examiners and then the PhD candidate to agree on the viva date and format. The viva is generally one to three months after submission. It can be online or in person; discuss and confirm arrangements with pgsupport.

3. There is usually a rehearsal beforehand to test the network and slide presentation. You can also request another time slot to practise presenting in the relevant meeting room.

4. Before the viva, the examiners meet privately, usually on the same day, though sometimes earlier. They then invite you into the meeting room to begin. Besides the two examiners, or three under special rules, there is an observer who manages the overall process and breaks and answers procedural questions. They generally do not speak during the examination itself. You can ask them if you have any questions.

5. Questions follow your presentation. Depending on the circumstances, one and a half to three and a half hours is common, although seven-hour vivas have occurred. Afterwards, you leave the meeting room while the examiners discuss the result. About 10-15 minutes later they invite you back and tell you the result in person.

6. You receive the examiners' written corrections report within ten working days. Depending on the outcome, make the required corrections within the specified period and submit them for confirmation by the examiner responsible.

7. Once the corrections are confirmed, upload the final thesis, completing the process.

(Information dated: 5 July 2024)

:::

### How to prepare for a viva {#如何准备好一场答辩}

::: {.contribution authors="ziwen-xie"}

Experience from the School of Science:

*Try not to squeeze all of this into two or three days. Spread it out so you can stay in good condition each day. Going into the viva in a good state is very important.*

**1. Read your entire thesis at least once, word for word, imagining you are a new reader and considering the following:**

1. Are any passages unclear?

2. Do you fully understand the concepts and can you explain them independently?

3. Do you understand the connections and differences between chapters, and the logic behind the overall order?

4. What is the logic behind the smaller sections within chapters and the sequence of experimental designs?

5. What does each experiment, or group of experiments, show separately or together? What conclusion can be drawn from each main chapter?

6. Do you fully understand why algorithms, models, and basic concepts in the cited literature work as they do? How do they relate to one another in the thesis and to your core experimental goals?

7. Are there errors in wording, figures, or tables that you had not noticed before and will need to correct later?

8. What is the purpose of the research? Why did you choose a particular method, and what advantages does it have over alternatives?

**2. After organizing those questions, break the thesis down chapter by chapter, including the abstract, for detailed analysis:**

1. Can you summarize all the background material in your own words?

2. What does each subheading communicate, and how coherent are the subheadings within the chapter?

3. What are the highlights or core logic of a particular experiment or experimental design?

4. How do the experimental results build on, run in parallel with, differ from, or otherwise relate to one another? For example, if experiment A shows a, experiment B shows b, and a provides the logical basis for B, the relationship is sequential. If a and b address the same direction or subject matter, A and B are parallel.

5. Why did you choose the experimental subjects and models? This includes why you did not use other related or similar subjects and models.

6. Based on the results, what could be attempted in future? This can involve many related questions: why you did not perform certain experiments, why particular future experiments would be useful, what they might show, their underlying hypotheses, and their practical difficulty. In other words, explain why you did not do them at this stage but did consider them.

7. The abstract should include the key results and novel contributions.

**3. Key points for preparing slides and taking the viva:**

1. You have twenty minutes in total, which can be divided into four parts: background, experimental setup, results, and conclusions. Allow roughly five minutes each, especially for the conclusion. The first three can be somewhat shorter because the examiners have already read the thesis.

2. Bring a printed copy of your thesis and take notes during questions. Taking notes also gives you a little breathing space.

3. Show the key figures, tables, and results in the slides, with brief statements of the conclusions.

4. You do not need to spend much time on problems encountered or emphasize future experiments and designs. Examiners may ask about them, or you may mention them in answers. Depending on the circumstances, omit them from the slides to save time.

5. Check that the slides work and that text and images are clear. During the advance test, rehearse as realistically as possible.

6. Remember to drink water during the viva, slowly and in small amounts. Beforehand, eat something energy-rich and easy to digest. If you cannot eat, have some chocolate or a refreshing drink. Arrive well in advance: getting familiar with the room helps you settle down. Remember to use the toilet beforehand too.

7. Your answers can draw on the whole thesis. A point in one chapter may connect to a later chapter, or future plans may relate to the final conclusions. If an examiner raises something you genuinely had not considered or done, say that you do not know. Ask them to specify in their feedback how to handle the issue or where to find the relevant information, so you know where to look when making corrections.

8. Usually each question and answer lasts at most three to five minutes. With two examiners, twenty questions from each is already quite a lot. The usual total is therefore two to two and a half hours, with a break in the middle, although once it starts you probably will not pay much attention to time.

**4. Questions beyond the thesis itself:**

1. How could artificial intelligence and ChatGPT inspire your research?

2. Could your research apply to other types of data, diseases, or fields? Why?

3. What shortcomings do you think your discipline has?

4. What is the biggest thing you have gained during your PhD?

5. If you could start again, would you still choose to do a PhD and this project?

Tip: the examiners often seem simply curious and interested in a conversation, so answer in a relaxed way. **Finally, according to figures shared by a pgsupport staff member, there has never been a failed viva since the university was founded. Do not worry too much: perform as you normally would, and good luck.**

**5. Ask your supervisor whether they can suggest possible questions and, if there is enough time, arrange a mock viva; this is optional. Also ask senior students about their vivas soon after they finish, since arrangements may change somewhat each year.**

(Information dated: 5 July 2024)

:::

## I want my degree certificate as soon as possible! Getting through graduation quickly {#我想尽快拿学位证如何速通毕业流程}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

In a hurry, in a hurry, always in a hurry: you are the king of impatience. Here is what every properly impatient person needs to know.

:::

### Documents proving completion and graduation {#毕业的证明文件}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

1. The Completion of Studies Certificate is issued by the XJTLU Graduate School. It states that you have submitted the thesis, passed the viva, and will be awarded the PhD at the graduation ceremony in month X of year XXXX. My example:

   ![Completion of Studies Certificate EXAMPLE](../../../assets/imported/Kai.Wu/Completion_of_Studies_Certificate_EXAMPLE.jpg)

   *For reference only, with a large EXAMPLE watermark to prevent unlawful misuse.*

2. The degree certificate, also called the PhD degree or degree certificate. Note: Liverpool awards degrees only at a **Liverpool** graduation ceremony, and Liverpool holds ceremonies only twice a year, usually on a day in July and a day in December. If you do not attend, you first receive an electronic certificate around the ceremony date. It has legal effect and can be used for credential recognition for Chinese-foreign cooperation programmes. The original then makes its leisurely way by post to XJTLU.

3. Credential recognition for a Chinese-foreign cooperation degree. You can apply once you receive the electronic certificate: <https://zwfw.cscse.edu.cn/>. With this recognition, the Ministry of Education recognizes your Liverpool degree in China.

First establish which documents your future company or employer accepts. The most flexible may accept Liverpool's confirmation email saying "Pass", with minor or major modifications, after the viva. Some accept the Completion of Studies Certificate. If they insist on the degree certificate, or even on the Chinese-foreign cooperation credential recognition, plan your graduation schedule especially carefully: certificates are issued only twice a year!

:::

### Degree certificate: the critical deadline {#学位证最关键时间节点}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

If you are sure there is no rush to obtain the degree certificate, you can ignore the rest of this section, because the Completion of Studies Certificate can be issued at any time.

Q: Can I graduate in July or December? What is the hard requirement?

A: The best approach is to check Liverpool's website directly or Google "liverpool phd graduation". In recent years, the requirement has been that Liverpool Library confirm receipt of your ~~ultimate absolutely-no-more-changes~~ final thesis before a specified date. For example, to join the Liverpool graduation ceremony on 15 July 2024, when the degree certificate would be awarded or mailed, Liverpool Library needed to confirm receipt by 25 June 2024. This is the final version approved by both your internal and external examiners. How do you get there? See the next section.

:::

### How long does each step take? Estimating the timeline {#sec.graduation.time}

::: {.contribution authors="kai-wu"}

The following is based entirely on graduates' experiences. New graduates, please contribute your own real examples generously.

Following the flowchart in [Official process and timeline](thesis-and-graduation.qmd#sec.official.flowchart):

1. ITS: once you submit it, focus on writing your thesis; the remaining work is for your supervisor and the Graduate School. Behind the scenes, (i) your supervisor proposes an internal and an external examiner; (ii) the Graduate School reviews them and may reject someone, for example because of a perceived conflict of interest. Your supervisor proposes replacements until the Graduate School is satisfied and one internal and one external examiner are agreed. Strictly speaking, you are not meant to know who they are until the thesis is submitted, and your supervisor must keep this confidential, so do not make things **too** difficult by pressing for names.

2. First thesis submission to viva: around 30 days, plus or minus 30. After submission, the XJTLU Graduate School (XGS) and Liverpool's Research Degree Administration (RDA) spend two or three working days processing the thesis and sending it to the examiners. Once the **internal examiner** receives it, they arrange the viva date. The date depends entirely on finding a normally two- to three-hour slot when you, the internal examiner, external examiner, and independent chair are all available. Thus the earliest possible date is three or four working days after submission. There is no prescribed latest date: it depends on finding a time for all four. If you are in a hurry: (1) contact your internal examiner soon after submitting and prompt them to arrange a date; (2) keep your schedule as free as possible for the next month or two so your own commitments do not delay it; (3) the internal and external examiners are difficult to change once appointed, but the chair is easier to replace. Sometimes a chair becomes unavailable a week before the viva and another teacher stands in. If the chair's availability is pushing the date far back, ask your supervisor early about a replacement. Normally, a viva 60 days after submission counts as very slow, although it has happened, reportedly when submission coincided with Liverpool strike action. Around 30 days is more usual.

3. Viva to final approval of the thesis: 0-180 days, typically three to four weeks. This varies greatly by viva outcome. (1) An unconditional pass means zero days: the submitted thesis is already final. (2) A pass with minor modifications is the outcome for the vast majority of students. (3) A pass with major modifications is another possibility; other, less fortunate outcomes are rare, ~~and perhaps your supervisor should fight the examiner they recommended~~. For outcomes 2 or 3, the examiners issue a written corrections report within ten working days, or two weeks. Personally, I suggest not hurrying them, because they have several forms and reports to complete. It then depends on how quickly you make the corrections. Follow Liverpool's emailed instructions for sending the revised thesis to the examiners. The next wait depends entirely on how quickly they respond and whether they are satisfied. Under the procedure, they can require further revisions until they are satisfied. To avoid repeated rounds, discuss the revised text carefully with your supervisor and aim to get it right in one go. This revision does not automatically become the final deposited version, so you can use colour or bold to highlight changes for the examiners.

4. Final approval to Liverpool Library confirming receipt: about seven days. This is purely administrative. RDA emails instructions to upload the final thesis after approval. In my case, the internal examiner told me they had informed XGS and RDA that the corrections were approved, and the upload instructions arrived four days later. Send the final thesis to Liverpool. A few days later, two in my case, Liverpool Library sends formal confirmation that it has been uploaded successfully.

5. There are some additional procedures, such as uploading a copy to XJTLU Library. I do not know whether this affects graduation, but it is best to complete it promptly once notified.

6. Electronic degree: the legally valid electronic certificate is issued within a few days either side of your ceremony date. Follow Liverpool's email instructions to view it at verify.liverpool.ac.uk.

7. Paper degree: if you attend the Liverpool ceremony, you collect it there. If not, it is officially posted to XJTLU after the ceremony, so you simply wait. In my case, I did not attend the 15 July Liverpool ceremony, and the paper certificate reached the Graduate School on 30 July. If you have already left campus, you can ask the Graduate School to post it to you, which I do not recommend: a lost original cannot be replaced, and you bear the risk.

(Information dated: 12 August 2024)

:::
